proposedDescription: Uroleucon picridis is an aphid associated especially with oxtongues in the genus Picris. Its wingless form is described as shiny reddish brown, with dark antennae and rear tubes but a yellow tail-like tip. Colonies around flowering shoots can make these otherwise easily overlooked insects easier to notice. Host identity is particularly useful here: closely related aphids have historically been confused, and research has separated another species from the broader picridis grouping. A confident identification needs the insect and its host examined together.
identification: Compare a close view of the aphid with the flowering host; color alone will not separate related Uroleucon.

proposedDescription: A swollen, papery-looking aphid can be the sign that a tiny wasp is doing useful work. Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the growing wasp develops there and eventually leaves through a round hole in the resulting aphid mummy. Adults are slender black wasps with long antennae. Growers use this species as a biological control agent, particularly against larger aphids such as potato and foxglove aphids. Its presence deserves a different response from that of a crop pest: the wasp is part of the community that can help suppress aphids.
identification: Look for aphid mummies and circular emergence holes; these indicate parasitoid activity but do not identify the wasp species on their own.
actions: When managing aphids, check for mummies and other natural enemies. Match any planned biological-control release to the aphid species with greenhouse or extension guidance.

proposedDescription: Green apple aphids gather where an apple tree is growing fastest: tender shoot tips, young leaves, and water sprouts. Their small green bodies can be easy to miss until leaves curl or sticky honeydew appears. In heavy colonies, that honeydew supports dark sooty mold on foliage and fruit, and feeding can slow young trees. The aphids overwinter as black eggs on woody growth. Lady beetles, lacewings, and other predators often keep them in check, so noticing aphids is a reason to inspect the whole shoot, including its natural enemies, before deciding what to do.
identification: Green aphids with dark rear tubes on tender apple growth resemble spirea aphids; glossy black winter eggs are not unique to this species.
actions: Monitor infested shoots and natural enemies, especially on young trees. Use local orchard or extension guidance if colonies are causing sustained injury.

proposedDescription: Apple-blossom cassia is a tropical flowering tree whose pink blossoms can make an entire crown look soft and airy. Its leaves are divided into paired leaflets, and the flowers are followed by long cylindrical pods. It is widely cultivated for this showy display, with several named forms that differ in details of leaves and flowers. Those differences matter when checking an escaped planting: a photograph of pink flowers may establish the general kind of tree without resolving the botanical form. Ornamental use alone does not establish that the species is invasive in every place it grows.
identification: Photograph a complete leaf, flowers, and pods; identification below species level may require stipule and sepal details.

Paired leaflets and long pods help place the tree in that group, but the older variety name indochinensis depends on finer botanical characters than flower color. Keeping that naming history visible is useful: two records with different names may describe the same botanical entity, while two similar-looking ornamental trees may not.

proposedDescription: Apple mealybugs often announce themselves as little patches of white wax on a tree. Beneath that powdery covering is a soft oval insect; mature females produce conspicuous white egg sacs. The species uses a range of woody hosts, and in orchards its honeydew can leave fruit and foliage sticky and encourage sooty mold. Mealybugs can also shelter in protected parts of a tree, making a quick glance at the leaves an incomplete inspection. Apple mealybug matters particularly in cherry production because it is associated with transmission of little cherry virus 2.
identification: Look for oval wax-covered insects and white egg sacs; distinguish them from the longer woolly coating of woolly apple aphids.
actions: Have suspected orchard infestations identified, especially near cherries. Ask local tree-fruit extension about monitoring when little cherry disease is a concern.

proposedDescription: Apple mint brings a fruity mint scent and soft, rounded leaves to herb gardens. The leaves are hairy and wrinkled, and pale flower spikes rise above the patch in summer. This is a creeping perennial: underground stems let a small planting expand steadily into neighboring ground, especially where conditions stay moist. That vigor is useful in a contained planting but can become a nuisance in an open bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it has been grown and naturalized elsewhere; garden spread should be described separately from documented ecological harm.
identification: Look for softly hairy, toothed, rounded leaves and dense pale flower spikes; scent supports identification but is not sufficient on its own.
actions: Contain a garden planting and check for shoots escaping its boundary. RHS recommends deep containers to limit spread.

proposedDescription: Apple of Peru looks at home in a flower border, with pale blue bells and a papery case around each fruit. It is a summer annual in the nightshade family, native to South America and naturalized in parts of the United States. Plants grow quickly in disturbed, fertile ground and spread by abundant seed. That combination has carried this ornamental into crop fields and other disturbed sites. Its lanternlike fruits can suggest an edible ground cherry, but the resemblance is misleading: this plant should not be treated as a food plant.
identification: Look for angular stems, broad unevenly toothed or lobed leaves, blue flowers with pale centers, and inflated fruit coverings.
actions: Avoid eating the fruits or other plant parts. If removing unwanted plants, act before mature seed is shed.

proposedDescription: Arabian jasmine is best known for the fragrance of its white flowers. This evergreen shrub can scramble over nearby support, carrying glossy oval leaves and blooms that may blush pink as they age. Cultivated forms range from simple flowers to richly doubled rosettes, so a garden specimen may look quite different from another plant of the same species. Despite its common name, Kew places its native range in Bhutan and India. Its long history in gardens and flower use is part of its story, but does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm where it has been introduced.
identification: Compare the glossy, simple leaves and fragrant white flowers; doubled cultivars can obscure normal flower structure.

proposedDescription: Arabian schismus is easy to overlook while it is a small tuft of fine green grass. In desert landscapes, the dry growth matters more: together with the similar Schismus barbatus, it can help fire cross the open spaces between shrubs. That changes a setting where bare ground would otherwise interrupt the fuel. This annual grows in disturbed ground and deserts, producing seed before drying down. Its resemblance to other small grasses makes careful identification important, especially when a management decision depends on separating the two Schismus species.
identification: Examine mature flower parts with a regional grass key; a photograph of fine leaves alone is not reliable.

proposedDescription: A flat bug can be an inhabitant of decaying wood rather than a feeder on living leaves. Brachyrhynchus membranaceus belongs to that less conspicuous world, where fungi are food. A USDA-hosted research record documents this Old World species in the Western Hemisphere. The existing species account also links it to cultivated bracket fungi, a reminder that an organism's role can change when its food becomes a crop. This is not evidence that it broadly damages healthy trees, and that distinction should remain clear when interpreting a sighting.
identification: A flattened brown bug around fungus-bearing wood needs expert comparison with other flat bugs.

proposedDescription: New growth on an Araucaria can host tiny aphids the color of a ripe apricot. Neophyllaphis araucariae has a broad, oval wingless form, usually only about 1-1.5 mm long, and feeds on the tree's young shoots. The specialist literature records it from several tropical and subtropical regions, including introduced settings, but its original home remains uncertain. The combination of host and bright yellow-orange color is a useful starting point. It should not be turned into a claim of serious tree damage without evidence from the affected plant.
identification: Check fresh Araucaria shoots for broad yellow to orange aphids; confirm with a specialist rather than relying on color.

proposedDescription: Araucaria black scale can look more like a dark speck stuck to a leaf than a living insect. The female shelters under a nearly round, brown-black cover that includes darker shed skins near its center. Despite the common name, Araucaria is only part of its host range: the scale has been recorded on many ornamentals and other woody plants. This makes checking the insects themselves important. A black spot on the right host can suggest an armored scale, but it cannot resolve the species without closer examination.
identification: Inspect dark circular leaf scales with magnification; an adult female may need slide-mounted examination.

proposedDescription: Aaron's beard prickly pear can grow from a cluster of pads into a branching, trunked shrub. Its gray-green pads carry tiny pale hairs and flexible white spines, while yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Native to Mexico, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Australia, where managers document spread from detached plant pieces and dumped garden material. Those Australian impacts should not be assumed everywhere, but the way the plant travels is useful to understand. A broken pad can be more than waste: it may be the start of another plant.
identification: Look for a trunked habit, finely hairy pads, and slender white spines; compare with similar prickly pears.
actions: Avoid spreading detached pads or dumping cactus material in natural areas. Use local disposal guidance and protect hands from spines and tiny barbed glochids.

proposedDescription: A busy ribbon of small brown ants along a wall or garden path may belong to Argentine ants. Workers are similar in size and move between shallow nests that can form part of a much larger network with many queens. Originally South American, this ant has become established in other regions and readily uses gardens and buildings. It feeds on sweet foods and tends honeydew-producing insects, which can complicate garden pest management. A trail in the kitchen is usually only the visible end of activity that extends outdoors.
identification: Workers are uniformly dull brown, about 1/8 inch long, with one waist node; confirm against other small household ants.
actions: Follow trails to locate entry points and nests, confirm the ant, and use local species-appropriate bait guidance if control is needed.

proposedDescription: The Argentine black and white tegu is a large, ground-dwelling South American lizard with a banded or mottled body and a powerful tail. Young tegus often have green heads that fade as they grow. Adults eat a varied diet of fruit, insects, eggs, and small animals, and retreat into burrows during colder weather. In Florida, established populations raise conservation concerns because researchers have documented predation on native wildlife, including alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises. Its adaptable habits help explain why an escaped pet can become more than an isolated garden visitor.
identification: Look for a large, sturdy black-and-white lizard with a long banded tail; young animals may have a green head.
actions: In Florida, photograph a suspected tegu, record the location, and report it to FWC. Never release a pet; use an approved surrender option instead.

Lower leaves are deeply divided, while the leaves higher on a flowering stem become simpler. Hairy stems carry little pale flowers followed by flattened, rounded pods with a notch at the tip. Plants can look quite different as they mature and lose their lower leaves, so a complete photograph is more useful than a single flower. Records of naturalization describe where it grows outside its original range; they do not alone measure ecological damage.

proposedDescription: Aonidiella taxus spends much of its life under a pale, translucent cover on an evergreen leaf. The female becomes reddish brown as she matures, and her color can show through the roughly 2 mm cover. Yew, plum-yew, and Podocarpus are recorded hosts. Feeding may produce yellow patches around the insect, especially on leaf undersides. Like other armored scales, its mobile young can spread within a plant, while transport of infested plants moves it farther. Several related scales look similar enough that a reliable species identification needs microscopic examination.
identification: Inspect needle and leaf undersides for pale rounded scales and nearby yellowing; slide-mounted females are needed for confirmation.

proposedDescription: False Meyer scale is a quiet-looking inhabitant of ornamental conifers. Its raised covers are oval to irregularly round and yellowish, becoming duller and browner with age. It has been recorded on arborvitae and related plants, sometimes at damaging levels. The colony can also support a small community of natural enemies: a 2019 study found parasitoid wasps and predatory mites associated with scales collected from Thuja. That observation is useful context, but it does not guarantee that natural enemies will control every infestation.
identification: Look for pale yellowish armored scales on conifers; distinguish them from similar scales through expert examination.

proposedDescription: Fly speck scale is aptly named: on a bromeliad, its small dark coverings can be mistaken for dirt. The insect has become a pest of bromeliad collections and greenhouse plants, where colonies can spoil the appearance of leaves. Mature females remain within a shed skin and produce mobile young rather than laying exposed eggs. Those crawlers can move between nearby plants, while the trade in living plants can carry the species much farther. Its native range is uncertain, so a precise origin story would overstate what the available evidence establishes.
identification: Examine persistent dark specks on bromeliad leaves with magnification; confirm they are scales and have the species identified.
actions: Inspect new bromeliads before adding them to a collection and keep suspect plants apart while seeking identification and local advice.

proposedDescription: Mining scale is unusually easy to miss because the plant itself can hide part of the insect's protective cover. It lives on woody hosts beneath pale, rounded armor that may become covered by outer plant tissue. Published accounts disagree about exactly how this happens, so its common name should not be read as proof that it tunnels like a leaf-mining larva. The species has been reported as a pest of woody ornamentals and several tropical crops. Close inspection of bark and identification of the scale are more useful than judging the severity of an infestation from a dark patch alone.
identification: Look for partly concealed rounded scale covers on bark; plant tissue can obscure their normal pale color.

proposedDescription: An orchid leaf with tiny brown, mussel-shaped marks may be carrying orchid scale. Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis lives mainly on orchids, though other host records exist, and can settle on leaves or stems. Feeding colonies may leave discolored patches and reduce the appearance of ornamental plants. Young crawlers move to fresh feeding sites, but moving an infested orchid can carry the insect much farther than it could travel on its own. The shell-like covering helps identify it as an armored scale; finer features are needed to distinguish this species from its relatives.
identification: Check both sides of orchid leaves and stems for narrow brown shell-shaped covers and nearby discoloration.
actions: Inspect orchids before trading or introducing them into a collection; keep suspect plants separate for identification.

It is distinct from Unaspis euonymi, the insect more commonly called euonymus scale. That distinction matters before choosing a response, since a plant's name alone does not identify its pest and seasonal activity can differ among scale species.
identification: Inspect the grooves between winged euonymus bark ridges for narrow brown scales; do not equate every euonymus scale with Unaspis euonymi.

Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about 1-2 mm long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. It occurs on a broad assortment of woody plants, often tucked into bark cracks. The specialist account notes how little its biology has been studied and reports little apparent damage in the California material it discusses. That is a useful limit: an inconspicuous introduced scale should not automatically be described as a major threat.
identification: Examine bark cracks in good light for narrow tan scales; reliable species identification requires microscopic examination.

The insect under the cover, rather than the plant's symptoms alone, is what allows a specialist to identify it.

Those features help locate a colony, but the distinction from other armored scales depends on much smaller anatomical details.
identification: Inspect upper leaf surfaces for flat translucent scales with pale margins; use microscopic confirmation for a species record.

Colonies are usually concentrated on citrus bark and larger limbs, with leaves and fruit involved when infestations are severe. Persistent heavy feeding can weaken a tree and contribute to branch dieback and splitting bark. Inspecting both the white male covers and the less noticeable females gives a much clearer picture than looking only for a white coating.
identification: Look for clusters of white narrow male covers mixed with dark female covers on citrus trunks and limbs.

It belongs to Old World tropical and subtropical vegetation, where its ecological role differs from that of populations introduced elsewhere. A thicket can be important to manage in one setting without making every plant of this species an alien invader.

proposedDescription: Arrow bamboo forms a leafy screen of upright canes and long, broad green leaves. What happens below ground is just as important: running underground stems can send new shoots beyond the original planting. It grows in meadows, river margins, and disturbed places, spreading both through seeds and underground growth. A patch can become dense enough to shade neighboring plants. Its expansion in parts of Europe has drawn attention to how soil conditions and seed germination influence its success. Those regional findings are useful background, but they do not establish the extent or severity of its effects in the United States.

proposedDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small cinnamon-brown scarab with the rounded shape of a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and emerge at night to chew leaves; their pale, C-shaped grubs feed underground on roots and young seedlings. Both stages use many garden and crop plants. Introduced from Asia, it has caused damaging infestations in some U.S. corn fields as well as landscapes. This two-part life cycle explains why ragged foliage and weak seedlings can point to the same insect.

proposedDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a small flowering plant with narrow leaves, coarse hairs, and flowers that may be red, yellow, white, or purple. Much of its effect begins before it appears above ground: the young plant attaches to grass roots and draws resources from its host. Crops such as corn and sorghum can be badly weakened. Its dustlike seeds can remain in soil for years, which is why introduced populations in the Carolinas have required persistent monitoring and control rather than a single season of weeding.

proposedDescription: Common asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle marked with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and their plump grayish larvae feed on asparagus, while rows of upright, dark eggs may be visible on the spears. Feeding can scar the edible shoots and damage the leafy summer growth that supports the next crop. The orange, black-spotted asparagus beetle is a different species. Checking the adult's markings and the affected plant parts helps connect a beetle sighting with the damage in a garden.

proposedDescription: Asparagus fern is a flowering asparagus relative with a soft, feathery appearance. Much of the fine green foliage consists of modified stems rather than ordinary leaves, and small pale flowers can be followed by bright red berries. Garden forms range from arching sprays to compact, upright plumes. These durable plants are grown in containers and warm-climate landscapes. Names in the nursery trade are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so the exact species should be checked before attaching a regional invasive-plant designation.

proposedDescription: Aspen leaf blotch miner is a tiny moth whose caterpillars spend their feeding stage inside aspen and cottonwood leaves. The larvae begin by taking sap, then eat leaf tissue between the surfaces. Their silk can pull the mined area into a raised fold, leaving a pale blotch or tentlike patch. The moth may never be noticed, while the leaf damage is easy to see. Recognizing this kind of mine helps distinguish an insect's sheltered feeding site from an ordinary leaf spot.

proposedDescription: Hairy fleabane, also called asthmaweed, is a fast-growing annual or biennial with narrow leaves and a covering of grayish hairs. Branching stems carry many small flower heads that develop fluffy, wind-carried seeds. It grows in orchards, fields, roadsides, and other open, disturbed places. Native to South America, it has become a widespread agricultural weed elsewhere, where it competes for water and other resources. Its hairy foliage and branching pattern help separate it from similar fleabanes, though close comparisons are often needed.

proposedDescription: This fleabane is an upright annual with a basal rosette, leafy stems, and many small flower heads. A Texas study found small colonies and young seedlings in gaps within coastal live-oak woodland, showing that it can establish beyond cultivated ground. Its flowers are much less showy than those of a garden daisy, and mature fruits carry fine bristles. Botanical sources have applied Conyza floribunda and related Erigeron names differently, so careful identification is important before combining records or making claims about its spread.

proposedDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen shrub or tree with a spreading crown and fine, jointed branchlets. Its tiny leaves hug the twigs, and clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear among the foliage. Deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty soils made it useful for shade and shelter in dry landscapes. It can also escape cultivation. In parts of Australia, dense riverbank infestations have altered water flow and soil salinity, illustrating why a hardy planted tree can become a management concern in some settings.

proposedDescription: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen climbing vine that can also make a thick carpet across the ground. Young shoots carry lobed leaves; flowering shoots have less-divided leaves and produce berries. Rooting stems expand a patch locally, while birds can carry seeds farther away. In invaded Pacific Northwest woodlands, dense ivy can cover native understory plants and add weight to trees. It closely resembles English ivy, and the species or cultivar should be confirmed when interpreting local weed guidance.

proposedDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect found on a wide range of trees and shrubs, including citrus, ivy, and ornamental evergreens. Its immature stages stay on leaves; the late immature cases are small, dark, and oval, and reliable identification requires magnification. Trade in infested plants can move it between regions. California's 2022 assessment reported no known significant economic or environmental damage there, while European observations likewise found limited injury. Finding the insect and demonstrating damage to its host are separate questions.

proposedDescription: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling perennial with coarse hairs and rounded leaves cut into several broad lobes. Small flowers, pink toward the tips and paler at the base, appear singly or in pairs. A thickened, branching root supports growth from season to season. In Australia it is associated with moist places such as creek banks, wet gullies, and forest margins. Its modest flowers and leaf shape help distinguish it from the more conspicuous plants commonly sold as garden geraniums.

proposedDescription: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with white-banded legs, pale lyre-shaped markings on its back, and a white ring around the middle of its long feeding tube. Its young use tree holes and rain-filled containers, including plant trays, buckets, and drains. Females bite people and other animals, sometimes during the day in shade. Recent detections in California show how this adaptable mosquito can become a neighborhood concern. Its markings matter because it closely resembles other introduced Aedes mosquitoes.

proposedDescription: Australian brake is a large, lacy fern whose fronds divide repeatedly into narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short, scaly base, and the fronds can move delicately in a breeze. Lines of spore-producing structures run near the underside edges of fertile segments. It grows in sheltered forest, streamside, and garden settings and has been cultivated beyond its Australasian range. Looking beneath a frond provides useful identification details that are easy to miss when seeing only its feathery outline.

proposedDescription: Australian cheesewood, or sweet pittosporum, is a shrub or tree with glossy leaves edged in gentle waves. Fragrant creamy-white flowers are followed by orange to yellow-brown capsules that open around sticky seeds. Birds help move those seeds away from planted trees. Although native to parts of eastern Australia, it has spread beyond its earlier range and become an environmental weed in some Australian forests and coastal scrub. Its familiar garden appearance can therefore mean different things depending on the local setting.

proposedDescription: Australian eelgrass, also called ribbon weed, is a freshwater plant with long, strap-shaped leaves rising from the sediment. Underground runners connect neighboring plants into tall underwater meadows. Small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks, which coil back underwater after pollination. Despite the name eelgrass, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations have been documented in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, where distinguishing it from other ribbonlike aquatic plants helps track changes in submerged vegetation.

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass earns its other name, windmill grass, from the long flower spikes radiating horizontally from each stem. It forms a low, dense clump with narrow leaves, and the small florets turn dark as they mature. In Australia it grows across several habitats and soil types, particularly red and black earths, and flowers in response to rain. The distinctive spoke-shaped head makes a flowering plant easier to recognize than a young clump; it should still be compared with other fingergrasses.

proposedDescription: Australian lovegrass, also known as paddock lovegrass, is a slender perennial that grows in loose tufts. Narrow leaves sit below an open, branching flower head made of many small, neatly stacked spikelets. A tiny fringe of hairs where the leaf meets the stem provides another identification clue. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it occurs in woodland and native pasture. Several unrelated concerns are attached to other plants called lovegrass, so the scientific name matters when deciding what a local observation means.

proposedDescription: Australian redcedar is a large deciduous rainforest tree with long leaves divided into many pointed leaflets. New foliage can flush reddish pink, while mature trunks develop scaly bark and substantial buttress roots. Small pale flowers are followed by woody capsules that release winged seeds. Its rich-colored, workable timber made it historically valuable and led to extensive logging in Australia. The shape also changes with its surroundings: forest trees can grow tall and straight, while open-grown trees develop broader spreading crowns.

proposedDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, usually mottled blue-green. Mature males have a soft, bright red patch along the outer edge of each large claw, a useful identification clue. It uses tropical streams, lakes, and billabongs in its native northern Australian range and is also farmed for food. It eats a varied diet that includes naturally occurring pond organisms and plant material. Movement for aquaculture has taken it beyond its home waters, where escaped populations can interact with local species.

proposedDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading perennial that can form broad mats above a deep woody root. Small gray-green leaves often look dusted underneath, and the seed is enclosed in fleshy reddish structures. Native to Australia, it was introduced elsewhere for uses including forage and erosion control. It tolerates dry and salty ground and has colonized disturbed coastal habitats in California. Animals can carry its seeds, helping explain how a plant close to the ground can establish new patches some distance away.

proposedDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and flat-topped woody seed capsules. Older plants can develop wonderfully twisted trunks and shaggy bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it tolerates salt spray and has been planted as a screen or windbreak. It has also naturalized beyond its original range and become weedy in some regions. Recent botanical treatments may use Gaudium laevigatum, so both names are helpful when matching observations with planting records or identification guides.

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a small, rounded leaf beetle with a dark brown shell mottled with black. Adults and larvae chew semicircular notches along eucalyptus leaf edges, sometimes leaving little more than a midrib. They often shelter beneath loose bark during the day and feed at night, so damaged leaves can be easier to find than the insects. Introduced into California, it can add stress to eucalyptus, although well-established trees often tolerate substantial feeding without needing treatment.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm is a small marine worm that builds a hard, pale tube and extends a feathery feeding crown into the water. In sheltered, often brackish settings, many tubes can accumulate into reeflike masses on structures or across the bottom. Those growths can change habitat and foul boats, pilings, and other waterfront surfaces. The common name is misleadingly definite: scientists remain uncertain about the species' original home. It has spread widely, but conspicuous reef formation and its effects vary between locations.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small herb with finely divided leaves and tiny, button-shaped flower heads held on slender stalks. The pale yellow or cream flowers lack the large outer petals of familiar daisies. Stems lie close to the ground or rise slightly and may root where they touch it. It grows in open grassy places, lawns, and roadsides. Native in Australia and New Zealand, it is a useful reminder that a plant described as a lawn weed can also belong naturally to a region's flora.

proposedDescription: Austrian pine is a substantial evergreen with stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees form a dense pyramid, while older trees develop a broad, rounded or flattened crown above stout branches. Brown cones point outward from the shoots, and mature bark becomes deeply furrowed. Native across parts of southern Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles are a practical first clue, while cone and bark details help distinguish it from other pines.

proposedDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial in the mustard family, with small four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that partly clasp the stem. Its nearly round seedpods help separate it from mustards with long, narrow pods. It grows along moist riverbanks and in disturbed places such as pastures, roadsides, and fields. Creeping underground roots allow a patch to expand as well as spread by seed. In parts of the western United States, it competes with desirable forage and native vegetation.
